People seriously need to be more aware of the cultural trends around them. Being an amateur futurist, I like to pay attention to the evolution of trends in the world.

The 'furry' subculture has its origins in the underground comix movement that emerged as part of the larger counter-cultural movement of '60s in response to the oppression of a corporate-dominated comic book industry and one of the many Great American Moral Panics triggered by the book Seduction of the Innocent. In the 1950s trends in comic books shifted to increasingly lurid and violent stories as their demographic grew up, which some psychologists and politicians exploited as an explanation for the apparent moral degradation of the youth culture. A comic book labeling code and set of content standards was imposed in the US to try and insure comics remained 'safe' for children, resulting in a general decline of the whole industry. Underground comix artists sought to free themselves from this creative oppression through independent publishing, protesting and parodying the infantilization of their medium by exploring increasingly adult themes. They produced comics featuring sex, drugs, violence, and psychedelia parodying the conventional sanitized comics with their use of superheroes and 'funny animal' characters inspired by the works of Disney and other childrens comics.

Visual communication relies on exaggeration and stylization to communicate. It has long been a tradition in comics to use animals to symbolize human personality traits, making it easier to communicate the nature of characters. And, that goes back into antiquity, with our various folktales, fables, and parables. Generally, artists have long found animals easier to draw than convincing human figures. And with such characters one can get away with criticizing or parodying things that would be too sensitive if depicted with humans. This carried over into animation. Few animation artists have ever been able to produce effective human characters without extreme stylization. And even early animation artists could use animal characters to get away with things that would never fly with human ones --such as Bugs Bunny's frequent drag routines or Pepe le Pew's rather rapacious sexual aggressiveness. So underground comix brought the tradition of the funny animal character into adult, and often erotic, themes.

With the comic book moral panic fizzling out by the '70s, a revival of superhero comics emerged as artists such as Stan Lee brought to that area more complex, adult, stories that delved into the personalities and moral dilemmas of characters. Together, underground comix and the new age of superhero comics brought the comic book medium to a general, adult, audience, resulting in a new 'independent comics' movement catalyzed by declining costs of printing technology. Comics fans became life-long fans, not giving up on their interest in the media in adulthood. Funny animals were no longer just kid stuff. So just as obsessed adult fans commonly sexualized their favorite superhero characters, so too did they sexualize the funny animal characters, who were still, really, just stylized human beings with exaggerated traits. Their animal traits just added to the novelty. Following the trend in the emergence of fan conventions for mainstream comics, science fiction, and anime, furry fans began creating conventions of their own, cultivating a dispersed community.

Furry came to the Internet largely through MUDs and MUCKs such as the famous FurryMUCK --given notoriety through tech culture media like Wired magazine and the now defunct Mondo 2000. This was followed by dedicated art boards for furry theme art. These new chat mediums allowed people to create their own virtual personas--avatars--that could express their personal fantasies. No longer limited to being fans of other people's characters, they could invent their own, whether or not they had any particular artistic skill. And, of course, a big part of the appeal of these online chat mediums was virtual sex through text. Cybersex, as it came to be called. This coincided with a digital erotica craze in the personal computing subculture inspired by expectations for the then emerging Virtual Reality technology. Eventually, this evolved to platforms like Second Life. Furry fans developed a large presence there and were key to its content development. More talented artists in the community realized they could start earning money from their fellow fans by selling their artistic skills to help other fans bring their avatars to visual life. This spread from the online scene to the convention scene, as furry fans started adopting 'fursonas', with a sort of parallel fantasy life of their own, whether or not they used them as avatars online. Having a fursona soon became a key aspect of the subculture. The standard badge of membership in the community. Naturally, some took that more seriously than others and some incorporated this fandom into New Age or mystical beliefs, imagining their fursonas as representing their 'true' spiritual identities.

As furry matured and grew with this online leverage, it became increasingly appealing to young homosexuals who found acceptance in the generally progressive community and found the practice of costume use in conventions appealing. Many homosexuals like to think of themselves as 'cute' and 'pretty' and cuteness is, of course, a virtue among funny animal characters. So the appeal is easy to understand. And, of course, we can't forget the 'bear' analogies either...

So that's where this cultural trend came from and how it evolved to what it is today.

I don't think we're too far apart in view here, just the perception of time. I never suggested that furry characters were ever a gay symbol or that there was any particular agenda being propagated. I suggested that the underground comix movement, followed by the independent comics movement, aided the medium, once limited to children's themes, to transition to adult themes and an adult audience. To be fair, one must also include the rise in US popularity of European comics (adult in themes going back into the '50s) inspired by Metal Hurlant magazine's republication in English as Heavy Metal and the active pursuit of english translation by publishers like Dargaud in the late '70s. Though some, like the Asterix comics, had long been in the US, the more adult types started appearing alongside independents in mainstream comic book stores in the '80s. As a result, funny animals in the context of adult themed stories became acceptable and increasingly popular and the fandom for comics in general extended into adulthood, largely among Gen-Xers. I think the issue of stylization is borne out in the scarcity of comics featuring non-stylized human characters outside the superhero genre. Superheroes have very distinctive costumes and body types. They don't have very distinctive faces --or rather didn't until pretty late in the history of the genre. (I think artists like Will Eisner and Joe Kubert were key to that, but such talents were rare. Kubert founded a school of comics art in Dover NJ that was highly influential on the evolution of the medium) Overall, more-or-less normal human characters in comics have tended to be in superhero, horror, romance, and crime theme comics with only superhero comics having long-persistent characters and series. Until you get to the independent comics boom, exceptions are very few and products of rare talent, like Europe's Tin Tin and Adèle Blanc-Sec. The contemporary aesthetic of superhero comics was largely established by Marvel and cemented in the late '70s book by Stan Lee, How To Draw Comics The Marvel Way, which was something of a blessing and a curse in terms of its impact on the medium and fandom.

I suggest that the furry fandom emerged in the early '80s primarily from that adult comics fandom, with some influence from the animation scene and SF&F literature. The superhero comic book resurgence you note, which started in the late '70s and '80s (what comic book fans sometimes refer to as the Bronze Age of comics, the 'silver age' being the period under the cloud of the Comics Code Authority), coincided with the rise of independent or alternative comics out of the underground comix scene. This itself produced a brief superhero animal craze with comics like Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles in '84. (you might recall such weird TMNTs clones as Adolescent Radioactive Blackbelt Hamsters, Geriatric Gangrene Jujitsu Gerbils, and Pre-Teen Dirty Gene Kung-Fu Kangaroos --no, I did not make those up...)

The rise of the furry fandom long predates Obama, Bush, and even Clinton, and was generating both positive and negative attention back then too. FurryMUCK appeared in 1990 and furry-theme BBSs go back to the early '80s-- some of these actually evolving into the first 'netwalla' (relating to the terms 'dabbawallah' and 'dishwallah') ISPs. The famous--or notorious--furry coliving home called The Prancing Skiltaire (named for an alien furry creature popular in the fanzines of the time much like today's 'sergal' characters) was founded with the creator of one of California's first ISPs. When they say 'furries make the Internets go', they aren't kidding.

I think you are correct that the anime cosplay fandom influenced the emergence of furry costuming or 'fursuiting'. Anime itself was also a wellspring of a lot of furry themed characters. It's true that many of the first fursuit wearers appeared at anime cons, about the time you noted, before there was an established furry convention circuit like in other fandoms. However, cosplay has generally been dominated by costuming based on established anime characters, not original characters as predominate among furry fans. I suggest that this idea of personal 'fursonas' originates online, in the medium of online chat and the notion of the digital avatar. The Japanese have their own fursuiting subculture, called 'kemono' (beasts) to distinguish it from cosplay, though that didn't actually emerge until after the turn of the century, some time after fursuiting became common in the US.

But anime too goes back a lot farther than you suggest. Anime also emerged as a coherent US fandom in the '80s, in the era of laser disks and VHS cassettes which was the primary means of exposing it to the US audience. A few early anime series appeared on US TV quite early--Kimba the White Lion was in the US in '65--but the contemporary anime fandom emerged when later more adult-themed anime series (like Captain Harlock, Galaxy Express, Urusaiyatsura) began making their way to the US by laserdisk and were transferred to bootleg VHS with added fan-created English subtitles. A number of fans actually created a small industry in this to finance their own personal trips to Japan to buy those laserdisks. This later moved online with the rise in internet use and the sharing of anime in file form, eventually compelling the larger Japanese media companies to start recognizing the existence of a US market and start dubbing anime in English for DVD distribution. Anime fan meets, based on group viewing of laserdisks or bootleg videos, started in the '80s, and soon evolved into a convention circuit emerging out of the venues for comic books and SciFi conventions. Though furries would similarly share comics, SciFi, and Anime venues, they had their own smaller informal meets and events. Just as conservative-minded comics and SciFi fans drove anime fans to their own conventions, so too did conservative-minded anime fans drive furries to their own conventions. (and, most recently, comics fans and furries driving My Little Pony fans off to their own conventions) Fandoms tend to create their own progressively more exclusive orthodoxies.

Fandoms interest me because they are one of the few genuine modern forms of large scale spontaneous social organization. Organizations not coerced by government (the fear of the gun) or religion. (the fear of death and hell) I believe they represent a major form of social organization in the future, with lifestyle communities like fandoms and academic/professional communities ultimately replacing national identity, town and city scale intentional communities and secular ashrams becoming the primary places where people live, and 'adhocracies' ultimately replacing corporations as we know them.
